finding.claim: SQL injection in /search: the user-supplied q parameter is interpolated into a SQL string via an f-string.
finding.sink: app.py:12 - db.execute(f"... LIKE '%{term}%'"), executed as raw SQL on the shared sqlite3 connection

trace.note: Attacker sets q to a raw string; no validation, length limit, or type check
term is concatenated into the SQL text inside single quotes; attacker closes the quote and appends their own SQL
fetchall() rows are returned as JSON, so UNION results (any column, any table in shop.db) reach the attacker

finding.guards_checked: No parameterization (lines 18 and 25 use ? placeholders, but line 12 does not). No input validation or allowlist. No auth gate. Flask does not sanitize query strings. The surrounding % wildcards do not prevent quote breakout. Example payload: q=x%' UNION SELECT name, sql FROM sqlite_master -- returns the schema, then table contents. Static analysis only; payload not executed.

verdict.guard_found: none. app.py:11 reads q with no validation; app.py:12 interpolates it into the SQL string with no parameterization, allowlist, or auth check. The ? placeholders at app.py:18 and app.py:25 are in other routes and do not cover /search. The route at app.py:9-10 has no auth decorator.
verdict.reason: The trace matches app.py:11-13: an anonymous request to /search (app.py:9-10, no auth) puts raw q into an f-string SQL query at app.py:12 and returns fetchall() rows as JSON at app.py:13, so a UNION payload such as x%' UNION SELECT name, sql FROM sqlite_master -- works because the query selects two columns.

finding.claim: Possible broken authorization in /by-owner: any unauthenticated caller can list products for any owner, with the owner taken from the query string.
finding.source: app.py:24 - request.args.get("owner", ""), fully attacker-controlled and unauthenticated
finding.sink: app.py:25-26 - SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE owner = ?, returned as JSON

trace.note: Route has no authentication decorator or session check
Owner identity comes entirely from the client
Parameterized query, so no injection, but it returns every product for the requested owner
Result returned to the caller unfiltered

finding.guards_checked: Parameterization is correct (no SQL injection). No authentication or ownership check against the requester. Whether this is a vulnerability depends on the data model: if owner is a private attribute this is an IDOR/enumeration issue; if it is a public storefront name, it is intended. The code cannot settle this; needs confirmation from the product owner.

verdict.guard_found: none. app.py:22 has no auth decorator or session check, and app.py:24 takes `owner` straight from the query string. app.py:25 is parameterized, so there is no SQL injection, but nothing checks the requester against the owner. The only files in the directory are app.py, so there is no schema or data-model context.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (app.py:22-26), and an anonymous caller reaches the unauthenticated, unfiltered owner lookup at app.py:25-26. Whether that is a vulnerability depends on whether `owner` is private data, and nothing in app.py or the directory settles that, so it needs the product owner's confirmation.
